title: Plurals and Possessives
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Standard English Conventions
summary: Scientist's, scientists or scientists'? Irregular plurals, its/it's, whose/who's, their/they're/there and joint possession — rules, method, worked examples and a 12-question practice quiz.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Plural and possessive questions are part of **Standard English Conventions** (about 26% of the scored Reading and Writing questions, usually 11–15 of them), in the skill **Form, Structure, and Sense**. The official skill list names **plural and possessive nouns**, and the pronoun pairs **its/it's**, **their/they're/there** and **your/you're**. This page also covers **whose/who's**, which follows exactly the same logic. Grammar questions usually appear after the reading questions in each module.

The stem is the usual conventions stem: **"Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?"** The four choices are the same word written in different ways — for example **scientist's / scientists / scientists' / scientist** — or a pair of words in which both may need an apostrophe, such as **colony's members / colonies' members' / colonies members**. You do not need to understand the science in the passage; you need to answer two small questions: **Is it possessive? Is it singular or plural?**
The three forms you must tell apart

**The "of" test:** turn the phrase around using "of". If you can say "the notebook **of** the scientist", you need a possessive. Then look at the noun after "of": if it is one (the scientist), write **'s**; if it is a plural ending in s (the scientists), write **s'**. If no "of" phrase makes sense, there is no ownership, so there is **no apostrophe**.

items: ✗ The **scientist's** met in Cairo. (Nothing is owned — just more than one scientist.)
✓ The **scientists** met in Cairo.
✗ Both **teams** coaches praised the players. (The coaches of the teams → possessive needed.)
✓ Both **teams'** coaches praised the players.
✗ Each **students'** project was displayed. ("Each" = one student.)
✓ Each **student's** project was displayed.

blocks.text: How to know if the noun is singular or plural
The passage always gives you a clue. Never guess — find the clue.

rows: a, an, one, each, every, this, that
numbers above one, many, several, both, these, those, all
a singular verb later (is, was, has)
earlier sentence: "a team of ecologists", "two orchestras"

blocks.text: Irregular plurals
Some nouns make their plural without -s. For these, the possessive is simply **plural + 's**. Never write "childrens'" or "peoples'" (unless you mean several nations — "peoples").

Academic nouns from Latin and Greek also appear in SAT science passages: **phenomenon → phenomena**, **criterion → criteria**, **datum → data**, **bacterium → bacteria**, **nucleus → nuclei**, **species → species** (same form). Their possessives follow the same rule: the bacteria's genes, a phenomenon's cause.
Pronouns: possessives have NO apostrophe
This is the rule that confuses most students. **Possessive pronouns never use an apostrophe.** When a pronoun has an apostrophe, it is a **contraction** — two words joined together.

rows: Say "it is". If it works, write it's.
**who's** = who is / who has — the writer **who's** visiting

blocks.text: **"its'" does not exist** in English. If you see it in a choice, cross it out immediately. The same is true of "their's" and "your's".

items: ✗ The museum reopened **it's** east wing. → ✓ The museum reopened **its** east wing.
✗ **Its** likely that the bridge will close. → ✓ **It's** likely that the bridge will close. (it is likely)
✗ The bees return to **they're** hive. → ✓ The bees return to **their** hive.
✗ The poet, **who's** collection won the prize, … → ✓ The poet, **whose** collection won the prize, …

blocks.text: Compound nouns, names and joint possession

items: **Compound nouns:** add 's to the last word. my **sister-in-law's** car; the **editor-in-chief's** decision. The plural changes the main word: two **sisters-in-law**.
**Joint possession (they share one thing):** put 's only on the last name. **Omar and Dina's** design (one design they made together).
**Separate possession (each has his or her own):** put 's on every name. **Omar's and Dina's** designs (two different designs). The owned noun is usually plural.
**Organisations and places:** they are singular. the **company's** profits; **Egypt's** population; the **university's** students.
**Singular nouns ending in -s:** add 's — the **bus's** route, **James's** essay. SAT questions rarely depend on this case.

blocks.text: The method for two-word choices
Hard questions put two nouns in each choice, for example **"the farmer's crops"** vs **"the farmers' crops'"**. Treat each word separately.

items: **Word 1:** Does it own word 2? (Usually yes — that is why the two words sit together.) Is it singular or plural? Choose 's or s'.
**Word 2:** Does it own the next word? Usually **no** — the next word is a verb or a preposition, so word 2 has no apostrophe. Decide only whether it is singular or plural.
**Check the verb:** "the crops **were** damaged" needs a plural; "the crop **was**" needs a singular.
Eliminate any choice with an apostrophe on a word that owns nothing.

blocks.text: Quick drill: fix the sentence
Decide whether each sentence is correct. If not, correct it, then open the answer.

items.q: The researcher's collected samples from three lakes.
items.a: Wrong. Nothing is owned ("collected" is a verb), so: The **researchers** collected samples from three lakes.

items.q: Both cities' mayors attended the conference.
items.a: Correct. Two cities own the mayors → plural possessive **cities'**.

items.q: The company announced it's new policy on Monday.
The womens' team won the final.
items.a: Wrong. Women is an irregular plural: **women's** team.

items.q: Each players' locker has a name tag.
Its been ten years since the bridge opened.
items.a: Wrong. It has been → **It's** been ten years.

items.q: Ahmed's and Laila's house is near the river.
items.a: Wrong if they share one house: **Ahmed and Laila's** house.

items.q: The scientist, who's research focuses on coral, spoke first.

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1: plural possessive**

In 2024, a team of ecologists surveyed honeybee colonies on farms near Fayoum. They discovered that the ______ health depended largely on the variety of flowers growing within two kilometers of each hive.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) colonies
B) colony's
C) colonies'
D) colonys'

blocks.title: Answer: C) colonies'
items: Of test: "the health of the colonies" → possessive. The team surveyed many colonies (plural), so the plural possessive "colonies'" is correct (C).
A is wrong: no apostrophe, so it is a simple plural and cannot own "health".
B is wrong: singular possessive, but the ecologists surveyed more than one colony.
D is wrong: "colonys" is not a word; the plural of colony is colonies.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2: a two-word choice**

Archaeologist Rania Saleh studies villages where the builders of ancient Egyptian monuments lived. In one village, she found that each ______ a small clay oven, suggesting that families baked their own bread.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) households' kitchen contained
B) household's kitchen contained
C) households kitchen contained
D) household's kitchens' contained

blocks.title: Answer: B) household's kitchen contained
items: "Each" means one household, so word 1 is a singular possessive: household's. Word 2, "kitchen", owns nothing (the next word is a verb), so it has no apostrophe. Choice B.
A is wrong: "households'" is plural, but "each" is singular.
C is wrong: "households" has no apostrophe, so it cannot own the kitchen.
D is wrong: "kitchens'" has an apostrophe but owns nothing.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3: its / it's**

The giant Pacific octopus is a master of disguise. It can change both the color and the texture of ______ skin in less than a second, a skill that helps it hide from predators among rocks and seaweed.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) it's
B) its'
C) their
D) its

blocks.title: Answer: D) its
items: The skin belongs to the octopus (one animal), so we need the singular possessive pronoun "its" — no apostrophe. Choice D.
A is wrong: "it's" = it is. "the texture of it is skin" makes no sense.
B is wrong: "its'" does not exist in English.
C is wrong: "their" is plural, but "the giant Pacific octopus" is singular (and the text uses "it").

blocks.text: **Worked example 4: joint possession**

The city library's new reading room for young visitors opened in March. It was designed by two architects, Omar Hegazy and Dina Farag, who worked together on every stage of the project. ______ design includes low shelves and floor cushions so that children can reach every book.
**Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?**

items: A) Hegazy and Farag's
B) Hegazy's and Farag's
C) Hegazy and Farags'
D) Hegazy's and Farag

blocks.title: Answer: A) Hegazy and Farag's
items: The two architects worked together on one design, so this is joint possession: 's on the last name only. Choice A.
B is wrong: 's on both names means separate possession — two different designs — but the text describes one shared design.
C is wrong: "Farags'" treats one person's name as a plural.
D is wrong: Farag has no possessive, so the phrase does not show that the design is theirs.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **The decoration apostrophe:** an apostrophe on a simple plural ("the scientist's met"). If nothing is owned, there is no apostrophe.
**The number trap:** "each" or "a" before the noun means singular even when the passage is about many things.
**The double apostrophe:** an apostrophe on the second word too ("farmers' crops'"). The second word usually owns nothing.
**its' and childrens':** forms that do not exist. Cross them out at once.
**its vs it's / whose vs who's:** possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe; read it's as "it is" to check.
**Joint vs separate:** "each developed a filter" → Fahmy's and Adel's filters; "worked together" → Fahmy and Adel's filter.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Ask the two questions in order: Does it own something? One or many?
Use the "of" test when you are unsure about ownership.
For pronouns, say the long form aloud in your head: it is, they are, who is, you are.
For two-word choices, decide word 1 and word 2 separately and check the verb.
These are among the fastest questions on the test — 20–40 seconds each.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Plurals and Possessives — Practice Quiz
blocks.intro: 12 questions in Digital SAT format. Untimed: for each one, ask "Does it own something? One or many?" before you choose.

questions.p: Before color printing became cheap, publishers could not afford to fill their books with bright pictures. As a result, many ______ books of the early twentieth century were illustrated with simple black-and-white woodcuts, which collectors now value highly.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "Children" is an irregular plural, so the plural possessive is "children's". "Childrens" and "childrens'" are not words, and "child" is singular and not possessive.
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Plurals and possessives

questions.p: The Saharan silver ant searches for food during the hottest part of the day, when its predators are hiding from the heat. Tiny hairs on ______ body reflect sunlight, helping the insect survive ground temperatures that would kill most other animals.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The body belongs to the ant (singular), so the possessive pronoun "its" is needed. "It's" means it is, "their" is plural, and "its'" does not exist.
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Pronoun forms

questions.p: Some stars seem to grow slightly darker for a few hours at regular intervals. Astronomers studying these distant ______ believe that the dimming happens when planets pass in front of them, blocking a small part of their light.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "These distant ___" is a simple plural that owns nothing (the next word is a verb, "believe"). So no apostrophe: "stars". "Star" is singular after "these".
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Plurals and possessives

questions.p: In the oases of Siwa, olive farming is an important source of income. A survey of olive growers found that the ______ most severely in years when spring temperatures rose well above the long-term average.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The survey covered many growers, so "farmers'" (plural possessive) owns "crops", and "crops" owns nothing, so it takes no apostrophe. A, C and D put an apostrophe on a word that owns nothing.
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Plurals and possessives

questions.p: The kakapo, a large flightless parrot from New Zealand, is one of the world's rarest birds. Because ______ active mainly at night and nests on the ground, the kakapo was easy prey for the cats and rats that settlers brought to the islands.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The clause needs "it is active", so the contraction "it's" is correct. "Its" is possessive, "its'" does not exist, and "they're" is plural.
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Pronoun forms

questions.p: A local orchestra held auditions last spring to fill two empty violin positions. Each ______ performance was recorded so that the judges could listen again and compare the candidates before making their final decision.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "Each" signals one candidate, and the performance belongs to that candidate, so the singular possessive "candidate's" is needed. A is plural possessive; B and C show no ownership.
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Plurals and possessives

questions.p: Desert locusts usually live alone, but heavy rain can produce a sudden burst of plant growth, and their numbers then rise quickly. Once the insects are crowded together, ______ able to form swarms containing millions of individuals.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The sentence needs a subject and verb: "they are able to form swarms", so "they're" is correct. "Their" is possessive, "there" refers to a place, and "its" is singular and possessive.
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Pronoun forms

questions.p: Engineers Tarek Fahmy and Yasmine Adel each developed a separate water filter for rural schools. ______ filters use different materials: one relies on layers of sand and charcoal, while the other uses a thin clay membrane.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Each engineer made a separate filter, so each name needs its own possessive: "Fahmy's and Adel's filters". A shows joint possession (one shared filter), which contradicts "each developed a separate" filter.
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Plurals and possessives

questions.p: Concrete roads and dark rooftops make city centers much hotter than nearby farmland. In a study of urban heat, ______ measured surface temperatures on rooftops across Cairo and found that white roofs stayed far cooler than dark ones.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The word is the subject of "measured" and owns nothing, so it is a plain plural with no apostrophe: "researchers". A and C are possessives; D is not a correct form.
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Plurals and possessives

questions.p: Novelist Farida Gamal spent four years interviewing older residents of Port Said before writing a single chapter. Gamal, ______ latest book follows three generations of one family in the city, says those conversations shaped every character.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The book belongs to Gamal, so the possessive "whose" is needed. "Who's" and "who is" mean who is ("who is latest book" makes no sense), and "whom" is not possessive.
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Pronoun forms

questions.p: In June, the city's transport agency and its environment agency published a study on summer heat. The two ______ joint report recommends planting shade trees along every major street and painting bus-stop roofs white.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: There are two agencies, and they own the report, so the plural possessive "agencies'" is correct. A is singular, B shows no ownership, D misspells the plural.
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Plurals and possessives

questions.p: A community history project in Alexandria has collected more than three hundred ______ memories of daily life in the city during the 1950s and 1960s. Volunteers recorded each interview and typed a full transcript for the project's online archive.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "People" is the plural of person, so its possessive is "people's". "Peoples'" means belonging to several nations, "peoples" and "persons" show no ownership.
questions.s: Form, Structure, and Sense: Plurals and possessives

blocks.title: Remember
items: No ownership = no apostrophe (scientists). One owner = 's (scientist's). Many owners = s' (scientists').
Irregular plurals take 's: children's, people's, women's.
Possessive pronouns have no apostrophe: its, their, whose, your. It's = it is; who's = who is.
Find the singular/plural clue: each, a, several, both, numbers, and the verb.
Shared ownership: Omar and Dina's. Separate ownership: Omar's and Dina's.
